newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Modest wage deals point to new S.African realism.
newsitem.headline: Modest wage deals point to new S.African realism.

text.p: South Africa has enjoyed a modest wage round this year with settlement levels held below 10 percent and agreement reached in most cases without significant industrial action.
Analysts said it appeared unions were moderating their demands in view of current economic realities, a shifting emphasis towards non-wage issues and a reassessment of their political clout.

Man-days lost for the nine months to end September increased to 1.35 million compared to 870,000 in the same period last year -- but the 1995 figures were exceptional in that they were the lowest since 1988, according to industrial relations consultants Andrew Levy and Associates.
Compared to 1994 and the three years before that, man-days lost so far in 1996 are still comfortably down and not expected to exceed two million by year-end.
Wage settlements across all industries averaged 9.9 percent in the nine months ending September 1996, compared with 10.4 percent in the first six months of the year.
Econometrix economist Tony Twine said lower inflation was a key factor, but the political landscape was also shifting.
"After two-and-a-half years of democratic rule, unions are coming to realise that they do not fulfil the function of being the sole political voice," Twine said.
Annual consumer price inflation, which was 7.5 percent in August, is expected to stay in single digits this year despite a sharp fall in the rand.

Head of policy at the union-backed National Labour and Economic Development Insititute, Ravi Naidoo, agreed the noticeable downwards trend in wage settlement levels was correlated with lower inflation.
But there was was also a new, less confrontational attitude across most sectors as some of the old political friction disappeared.
Many pre-1994 strikes were politically-motivated and not solely related to workplace issues, he noted.

"With the new Labour Relations Act coming into place next month, there is a sense that both employers and workers need to change to take into account recent legislative and political developments," he said.
Naidoo said wage restraint was also linked to greater emphasis on broader non-wage issues such as health and retirement benefits.
Wage settlements in the key mining industry, concluded in mid-September, ranged from eight to 10 percent for gold mines and from 8.38 to 10.75 percent at collieries.
In the motor industry, agreement was reached at the central level on an 8.5 percent increase, excluding Mercedes Benz, which negotiated a plant level agreement at a rate of 5.9 percent.
Other wage settlements reached with major unions include 9.2 percent with the National Union of Metalworkers of South Africa and 9.1 percent with the South African Clothing and Textile Workers Union.
Professor of Politics at the University of the Western Cape David Welsh said there appeared to be a subtle shift in union perceptions of their bargaining position.

"It may be that unions have recognised that in relation to the ANC (African National Congress) they are the junior partner while the other arguable point is that they are a peculiarly privileged segment of the working class and exaggerated wage claims lead to diminished employment," he said.

The fact that the country's main labour union federation, the Congress of South African Trade Unions had softened its stance on privatisation and was co-operating with the government also pointed to less industrial strife, according to Andrew Levy Associates.

Cosatu general secretary Sam Shilowa last month put forward the federation's latest stance on privatisation, arguing certain state assets could be sold off provided government remained a majority shareholder in strategic sectors.
